# Linear models in R {.unnumbered} In hour 1 you saw why the t-statistic, the estimate divided by its standard error, can be compared with the t-distribution instead of building a full permutation null distribution, and drew a comparison of two group means as a line. Here you fit the linear model in R and read its coefficient table, which reports those coefficients with their t-statistics and p-values. The data are the same paired differences you have worked with since Session 2: the height of the cross-fertilised plant minus the height of the self-fertilised plant within each pair. ## The paired differences {#sec-s4-data} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: inspect the paired differences** :::: ::::{.task-container} Run the code below to see the fifteen paired differences. These are the same values you used in Sessions 2 and 3. :::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} darwin_diff |> select(pair, cross, self, difference) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| pair| cross| self| difference| |----:|------:|------:|----------:| | 1| 23.500| 17.375| 6.125| | 2| 12.000| 20.375| -8.375| | 3| 21.000| 20.000| 1.000| | 4| 22.000| 20.000| 2.000| | 5| 19.125| 18.375| 0.750| | 6| 21.500| 18.625| 2.875| | 7| 22.125| 18.625| 3.500| | 8| 20.375| 15.250| 5.125| | 9| 18.250| 16.500| 1.750| | 10| 21.625| 18.000| 3.625| | 11| 23.250| 16.250| 7.000| | 12| 21.000| 18.000| 3.000| | 13| 22.125| 12.750| 9.375| | 14| 23.000| 15.500| 7.500| | 15| 12.000| 18.000| -6.000|
::: ::: ## Fit the intercept-only model {#sec-s4-fit} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: predict the intercept** :::: ::::{.task-container} Before running any code, write down your prediction. You have computed the mean of these differences before. What value do you expect the intercept to be? :::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lsmodel1 <- lm(difference ~ 1, data = darwin_diff) ``` ::: The formula `difference ~ 1` means "fit an intercept only." The intercept is the mean of the paired differences. The coefficient table tests whether that mean differs from zero — the same question the permutation test in Session 3 answered. ## Read the coefficient table {#sec-s4-summary} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: read the summary output** :::: ::::{.task-container} Run the code below. Compare the intercept with your prediction, then answer: 1. What does the estimate represent? 2. What does the t-value represent, and how does it relate to the ranking exercise from hour 1? 3. Is there evidence that the mean difference is not zero?
1. The estimate is the mean of the fifteen paired differences — the average advantage of cross-fertilisation over self-fertilisation within a pair. 2. The t-value is the estimate divided by its standard error. A larger absolute t-value means the estimate is further from zero in standard-error units, just as in the ranking exercise. It matches the value you calculated by hand in hour 1 (about 2.15). 3. The p-value is 0.0497, just below 0.05. The exact permutation p-value from hour 1 was 0.053, just above it; your Session 3 simulations estimated that value. The two methods answer the same question and give almost the same answer: the evidence is borderline either way, and 0.05 should not be treated as a bright line.
:::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Base R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(lsmodel1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = difference ~ 1, data = darwin_diff) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -10.9917 -1.2417 0.3833 3.0083 6.7583 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 2.617 1.218 2.148 0.0497 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 4.718 on 14 degrees of freedom ``` ::: ::: ## Broom ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} broom::tidy(lsmodel1, conf.int = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| conf.low| conf.high| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:| |(Intercept) | 2.616667| 1.218195| 2.147988| 0.0497029| 0.0038992| 5.229434|
::: ::: ::: ## Confidence interval from the model {#sec-s4-ci} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: obtain and interpret the confidence interval** :::: ::::{.task-container} Run the code below. The output is a 95% confidence interval for the mean paired difference. 1. Does this interval include zero? 2. Compare it with the confidence interval you computed in Session 2 (about 0.23 to 5.0 inches). Why is the model's interval wider?
1. No, but only just: the lower limit is about 0.004 inches. This is consistent with a p-value just below 0.05. 2. You met this in hour 1. In Session 2 you used estimate ± 1.96 × SE. The model uses estimate ± 2.14 × SE. The larger multiplier comes from the t-distribution with 14 degrees of freedom: because the SE is itself estimated from only fifteen values, the interval is widened to allow for that extra uncertainty. As the sample size grows, the multiplier gets closer to 1.96.
:::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Base R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} confint(lsmodel1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 2.5 % 97.5 % (Intercept) 0.003899165 5.229434 ``` ::: ::: ## Broom ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} broom::tidy(lsmodel1, conf.int = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| conf.low| conf.high| |:-----------|--------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:|---------:| |(Intercept) | 2.616667| 1.218195| 2.147988| 0.0497029| 0.0038992| 5.229434|
::: ::: ::: The multiplier the model uses for a 95% interval with 14 degrees of freedom: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qt(0.975, df = 14) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2.144787 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## A simple write-up From the linear model on paired differences: "Cross-fertilised maize plants were taller on average than self-fertilised plants, with a mean paired difference of 2.62 inches (95% CI: 0.004, 5.23; t(14) = 2.15, p = 0.0497)." Note: the degrees of freedom are 14 (fifteen pairs minus one), not 28. Match the values to your output. ::: ## Compare with the one-sample t-test {#sec-s4-compare-ttest} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: confirm the equivalence** :::: ::::{.task-container} Run the code below. Compare the p-value from `t.test()` with the p-value from `summary(lsmodel1)`. They should be identical. This confirms that the intercept-only linear model on paired differences is the same test as a one-sample t-test. The linear model is the more general framework. :::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(darwin_diff$difference, mu = 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` One Sample t-test data: darwin_diff$difference t = 2.148, df = 14, p-value = 0.0497 alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: 0.003899165 5.229434169 sample estimates: mean of x 2.616667 ``` ::: ::: ## Composition task: fit the unpaired model {#sec-s4-composition} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: write an `lm()` call for the unpaired comparison** :::: ::::{.task-container} You have just fitted a model that respects the paired design: ```r lsmodel1 <- lm(difference ~ 1, data = darwin_diff) ``` Now write an `lm()` call that ignores the pairing entirely: model height as a function of fertilisation type, using the original `darwin` data frame. Assign the result to `lsmodel2` and run `summary()` on it.
The response is `height`, the predictor is `type`, and the data are `darwin`. The formula takes the form `response ~ predictor`.
```r lsmodel2 <- lm(height ~ type, data = darwin) summary(lsmodel2) ```
:::: ::: By default, R uses the first level of `type` in alphabetical order, Cross, as the **reference level**. In `lsmodel2` the intercept is the mean height of the cross-fertilised plants, and `typeSelf` is the difference between the self-fertilised mean and that reference. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: compare the two models** :::: ::::{.task-container} Look at the coefficient table for `lsmodel2`. Compare the estimates with the line you drew in hour 1, and the standard error with your hour 1 prediction. 1. What does the `typeSelf` coefficient estimate? Is this the same quantity as the intercept of `lsmodel1`? 2. Compare the standard error and p-value for `typeSelf` with those for the intercept of `lsmodel1`. Which model gives the smaller standard error? Does that make it the better model?
1. The `typeSelf` coefficient estimates the difference in mean height between self-fertilised and cross-fertilised plants — the same quantity as the intercept of `lsmodel1`, but with the opposite sign (Self minus Cross rather than Cross minus Self). The absolute value is the same. 2. The unpaired model gives the smaller standard error (about 1.07, against 1.22) and the smaller p-value (about 0.021, against 0.0497). In Darwin's maize, the heights of the two plants in a pair were slightly negatively correlated, so pairing did not reduce the variation. The unpaired model is still the wrong model: it treats the thirty plants as thirty independent observations, which the design says they are not. Choosing a model because it gives a smaller p-value is a form of p-hacking.
:::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Why pairing matters Darwin grew his plants in matched pairs, one cross-fertilised and one self-fertilised, so that the two plants in a pair shared growing conditions. Pairing is designed to remove variation between pairs and isolate the effect of fertilisation type. In Darwin's maize it did not reduce the standard error, but the paired analysis is still the correct one, because it matches how the data were generated. The lesson: a model should respect the design that generated the data, whichever model gives the smaller p-value. ::: ## Exit ticket {#sec-s4-hour2-exit} :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} **Task: exit question** :::: ::::{.task-container} Write your answer on paper before you leave. You fit > `lm(wing_length ~ species, data = df)` and get three coefficients > for species (plus the intercept). Is the model answering the > question you intended, and what should you do before fitting it? :::: ::: ## Reading ### Library - The New Statistics with R, 2nd Edition, **Chapter 6** by Andy Hector ### Online - [Everything is a Linear Model](https://danielroelfs.com/posts/everything-is-a-linear-model/), by Daniel Roelfs - [Common statistical tests are linear models](https://lindeloev.github.io/tests-as-linear/), by Jonas Kristoffer Lindeløv - *Covers more than we got to today*
